objective: In 120-180 words, what does the original-versus-randomly-permuted electricity-data comparison in Table 2 show about the different roles of calibration-residual weighting and weighted least-squares fitting in coverage and interval width? Interpret the comparisons against the 90% target, distinguish the exchangeable permuted control from the ordered data, and explain why this empirical result is not a universal 90% coverage guarantee under arbitrary distribution drift.
A: Table 2 distinguishes coverage recovery through calibration weighting from interval shortening through fitting, at a 90% target. On ordered electricity data, keeping least squares fixed while weighting calibration residuals raises temporal-average coverage from 85.2% to 89.0%, but increases mean width from 0.565 to 0.606. With calibration weighting retained, weighted least squares gives 89.3% coverage and width 0.527: narrower intervals accompany slightly higher observed coverage, although both weighted methods remain below target. The randomly permuted, exchangeable version of the same data changes that comparison. Unweighted least squares, residual-weighted least squares, and residual-weighted weighted least squares attain 89.9%, 90.8%, and 90.8% coverage, with widths 0.639, 0.652, and 0.663, respectively. Thus weighted fitting provides no width advantage in the control, and weighting increases variability. These averages support complementary calibration and fitting roles on ordered data, not coverage at every prediction time. Arbitrary drift can produce a large weighted total-variation penalty between original and swapped residual distributions; the empirical gains therefore do not establish universal 90% coverage.
B: Table 2 shows that, on ordered electricity data, improving coverage through calibration weighting need not require wider intervals once fitting also changes. At a 90% target, ordinary full conformal with least squares (CP+LS) averages 85.2% coverage and width 0.565. Weighting only calibration residuals (NexCP+LS) raises coverage to 89.0% but increases width to 0.606. Adding weighted least-squares fitting (NexCP+WLS) retains higher coverage, 89.3%, while reducing width to 0.527, below both alternatives; neither weighted method reaches 90% on average. Uniform random permutation makes the data exchangeable: the respective coverages are 89.9%, 90.8%, and 90.8%, with widths 0.639, 0.652, and 0.663. The fitting change thus offers no width advantage in this control, and weighted procedures have greater variability. This contrast supports distinct calibration and fitting benefits in the ordered setting, not a generally narrower weighted method. These averages across prediction times neither establish coverage at every time nor universal 90% coverage under drift, because the theorem's weighted swapped-residual total-variation penalty may be large.

objective: In 120-180 words, what does the original-versus-randomly-permuted electricity-data comparison in Table 2 show about the different roles of calibration-residual weighting and weighted least-squares fitting in coverage and interval width? Interpret the comparisons against the 90% target, distinguish the exchangeable permuted control from the ordered data, and explain why this empirical result is not a universal 90% coverage guarantee under arbitrary distribution drift.
A: Table 2 separates improved coverage from narrower intervals in electricity-transfer prediction. In the original time order, unweighted full conformal with least squares yields 85.2% coverage and mean width 0.565. Keeping least squares but weighting calibration residuals raises coverage to 89.0% while increasing width to 0.606; adding weighted least-squares fitting gives 89.3% and width 0.527. Thus calibration weighting moves coverage toward the 90% target at a width cost, whereas weighted fitting produces narrower intervals with similar coverage in this setting. Neither weighted method reaches the target. In the randomly permuted, exchangeable control, these three methods have coverage 89.9%, 90.8%, and 90.8%, with widths 0.639, 0.652, and 0.663, respectively. The weighted-fitting width advantage does not persist after random permutation. These time-averaged comparisons neither establish coverage at every time point nor guarantee 90% coverage under arbitrary drift. For the randomized construction, a near-nominal coverage lower bound requires a small weighted swapped-residual total-variation term.
B: Table 2 distinguishes improved calibration from narrower intervals on the ordered electricity-transfer data. Keeping least-squares fitting fixed, weighting calibration residuals raises coverage from 85.2% to 89.0% but increases mean width from 0.565 to 0.606. Retaining residual weighting and adding weighted least-squares fitting gives 89.3% coverage and reduces width to 0.527, below the unweighted baseline's 0.565. Thus calibration weighting improves coverage here at a width cost, while weighted fitting offsets that cost; neither weighted method reaches the 90% target. Uniformly permuting the same data creates an exchangeable control: coverage is 89.9%, 90.8%, and 90.8% for unweighted, residual-weighted, and additionally weighted-fit methods, respectively, with widths 0.639, 0.652, and 0.663. The observed width advantage disappears after permutation. These time-averaged comparisons do not guarantee 90% coverage under arbitrary drift: the theoretical lower bound is near nominal only when the weighted total-variation discrepancy between original and swapped residual-vector distributions is small.

objective: In 110-160 words, how does the proof of Theorem 2b turn a data-independent weighted random swap into a miscoverage bound for full conformal prediction with a nonsymmetric fitting algorithm? Explain the weighted mass bound for high-residual indices and the comparison of swapped and original residual distributions, including the roles of prespecified calibration weights in [0,1] and fixed algorithm tags.
A: Unequal calibration weights and order-sensitive fitting obstruct the usual exchangeable-residual argument. Theorem 2b prespecifies weights w_i in [0,1] and algorithm tags t_i, normalizes the weights with unit test weight, and draws K independently of the data using these probabilities. Swap observation K with the test point before fitting, retaining positional tags; at the true test label, the test residual occupies position K in the swapped residual vector. Residuals above the swapped vector's weighted (1-alpha)-quantile carry total normalized weight at most alpha. The rejection test is unchanged if its threshold places the test weight at infinity; because w_i <= 1, this threshold dominates the swapped-vector quantile. Miscoverage thus requires K to be a high-residual index. Independence permits averaging over K. Comparing each swapped residual law with the original adds its total-variation distance; the original-law weighted mass is at most alpha. Miscoverage is consequently bounded by alpha plus the weighted distances.
B: Theorem 2b fixes calibration weights w_i in [0,1] and algorithm tags before observing data. Normalize the weights with a unit test weight and draw K independently using these probabilities. At the true label, fitting after swapping observations K and n+1 while keeping tags fixed puts the test residual at index K of R(Z^K). For any residual vector r, indices S(r) strictly above its weighted (1-alpha)-quantile have normalized weight at most alpha. Because the test weight dominates every calibration weight, the prediction cutoff with test mass at infinity is no smaller than the cutoff for R(Z^K); miscoverage therefore implies K belongs to S(R(Z^K)). Independence expresses this event probability as a weighted sum over K. Replacing each swapped residual law by the original costs at most its total-variation distance. The original-law sum is at most alpha, yielding miscoverage at most alpha plus the weighted residual-distribution penalty.

objective: In 150-200 words, what is the paper's central contribution to full conformal prediction when data exchangeability or model-fitting symmetry fails? Explain how fixed calibration weights, fixed algorithm tags, and a data-independent randomized swap connect a finite-sample coverage bound to the empirical coverage/interval-width tradeoff, distinguishing exchangeable-data validity from near-nominal coverage under nonexchangeability when the weighted swapped-residual total-variation term is small.
A: Full conformal prediction ordinarily relies on exchangeable data and symmetric fitting. We extend it with fixed calibration weights in [0,1], fixed algorithm tags, and a data-independent weighted random swap. Weights emphasize observations expected to resemble the test distribution; tags enable order-sensitive fitting. The swap connects miscoverage to high-residual indices, whose total normalized weight is at most alpha for any residual vector. Comparing original and swapped residual-vector distributions then gives finite-sample coverage at least 1 - alpha minus their weighted total-variation discrepancy. Under exchangeability this penalty vanishes, restoring nominal validity even with nonsymmetric fitting; otherwise, a small penalty limits undercoverage. When residuals are distinct, small discrepancy and normalized test weight also limit overcoverage. Related bounds cover split conformal and jackknife+, the latter with baseline 1 - 2 alpha. In simulations and electricity data, calibration weighting improves coverage, whereas weighted least-squares fitting can narrow intervals. On ordered electricity data, calibration weighting raises coverage from 85.2% to 89.0% but widens intervals; adding weighted fitting yields 89.3% coverage and narrower intervals. Both remain below the 90% target, and the width advantage disappears under random permutation. Election-data improvements also remain below target.
B: Full conformal prediction usually relies on exchangeable data and symmetric fitting, excluding order-sensitive predictors and leaving coverage vulnerable to drift. Our extension separates two roles: fixed calibration weights in [0,1] emphasize observations expected to resemble the test point, while fixed algorithm tags encode information used by nonsymmetric fitting. A data-independent weighted random swap moves the candidate test point to a sampled position before fitting, with tags retained at their positions. This makes miscoverage imply membership in a high-residual set with weighted mass at most alpha. Comparing swapped and original residual-vector distributions yields finite-sample coverage at least 1 - alpha minus their weighted total-variation discrepancy. Under exchangeability this discrepancy vanishes even with nonsymmetric fitting; otherwise, a small discrepancy bounds undercoverage, not exact nominal validity. With distinct residuals, small discrepancy and normalized test weight also limit overcoverage; related bounds extend to split conformal and jackknife+. Simulations and electricity data distinguish calibration gains from width gains: on ordered electricity data, residual weighting improves coverage but widens intervals, whereas adding weighted fitting gives 89.3% coverage and narrower intervals than unweighted fitting, against a 90% target. Permutation removes the width advantage, and election-data coverage also remains below target.

objective: In 150-200 words, what is the paper's central contribution to full conformal prediction when data exchangeability or model-fitting symmetry fails? Explain how fixed calibration weights, fixed algorithm tags, and a data-independent randomized swap connect a finite-sample coverage bound to the empirical coverage/interval-width tradeoff, distinguishing exchangeable-data validity from near-nominal coverage under nonexchangeability when the weighted swapped-residual total-variation term is small.
A: Nonexchangeable observations and order-sensitive model fitting break the usual symmetry argument for full conformal coverage. We extend split and full conformal prediction and jackknife+ by separating calibration weighting from tagged model fitting. Prespecified calibration weights in [0,1] emphasize observations believed comparable to the test point, while fixed tags let fitting exploit order. For full conformal prediction, a data-independent swap exchanges the test observation with an index sampled using normalized calibration weights and unit test weight before fitting. The swap links miscoverage to high-residual indices whose weighted mass cannot exceed alpha, without requiring symmetric fitting. Coverage is therefore at least 1-alpha minus a weighted sum of total-variation distances between original and swapped residual distributions; jackknife+ instead starts from 1-2alpha. Exchangeability eliminates this penalty, preserving validity. Under nonexchangeability, a small penalty limits undercoverage; distinct residuals and a small normalized test weight also limit overcoverage. Nonexchangeable simulations and ordered electricity data support complementary roles: calibration weighting improves coverage but widens intervals, whereas weighted fitting can shorten them. That width advantage disappears in the exchangeable, randomly permuted electricity control. Election coverage improves but remains below 90%, underscoring that arbitrary drift is not covered by a nominal guarantee.
B: We extend full conformal prediction to nonexchangeable data and nonsymmetric model fitting, with related split conformal and jackknife+ procedures. Prespecified calibration weights in [0,1] reduce reliance on observations considered less comparable to the test point, while fixed algorithm tags allow fitting to use order or regression weights. A data-independent swap, sampled with probabilities proportional to these weights and a unit test weight, makes miscoverage imply membership in a high-residual set of normalized weight at most alpha. Comparing swapped and original residual distributions then gives finite-sample coverage at least 1-alpha minus their weighted total-variation distances, without requiring fitting symmetry. Exchangeability eliminates this penalty; under nonexchangeability, a small penalty bounds undercoverage, with distinct residuals and small normalized test weight additionally limiting overcoverage. Experiments distinguish calibration from fitting: on ordered electricity data, residual weighting improves coverage but widens intervals, whereas weighted least squares narrows intervals while retaining the coverage improvement. Random permutation removes this width advantage, and election coverage improves but remains below the 90% target. Thus the guarantee depends on residual-distribution changes, while empirical benefits depend on the evaluated ordering and weighting choices.

objective: In 110-160 words, how does the proof of Theorem 2b turn a data-independent weighted random swap into a miscoverage bound for full conformal prediction with a nonsymmetric fitting algorithm? Explain the weighted mass bound for high-residual indices and the comparison of swapped and original residual distributions, including the roles of prespecified calibration weights in [0,1] and fixed algorithm tags.
A: Unlike symmetric fitting, nonsymmetric fitting need not produce exchangeable residuals. Prespecify calibration weights w_i in [0,1] and fixed tags; normalize by D = 1 + sum_i w_i, giving the test point weight 1/D. Draw K independently using these weights and swap observation K with the candidate test observation, keeping tags at their positions. At the true response, miscoverage implies that the test residual, now at index K, exceeds the swapped vector's weighted (1 - alpha)-quantile. The implication follows by replacing the test residual by infinity in the quantile and noting that each calibration weight is at most the test weight. For every residual vector, these high-residual indices carry normalized mass at most alpha. Independence allows averaging over K; comparing each swapped-vector event with its original-vector counterpart adds at most their total-variation distance. Hence miscoverage is bounded by alpha plus the weighted residual-distribution discrepancy, without algorithm symmetry or stability.
B: Weighted quantiles and nonsymmetric fitting prevent the usual exchangeable-rank argument. Prespecify calibration weights w_i in [0,1] and algorithm tags; normalize by D = 1 + sum_i w_i, assigning test weight 1/D. Draw K independently of the data using these normalized weights, swap the candidate test point with position K, and fit with tags fixed at their positions. At the true response, the test residual becomes entry K of the swapped-sequence residual vector. Replacing the test residual by infinity and using the test weight's dominance over calibration weights show that miscoverage implies entry K exceeds that vector's weighted (1 - alpha)-quantile. Such high-residual indices have total normalized weight at most alpha for every vector. Independence allows averaging their probabilities over K. Total variation bounds the change in each probability between swapped and original residual-vector distributions, yielding miscoverage at most alpha plus the weighted discrepancy, without fitting symmetry or stability.
